scenes.name: El pop de papá y mamá
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los adultos compraban LPs (a 32 chelines frente a los 6 de un single) y también muchos singles, de modo que la lista británica de 1965 era esquizofrénica: los Stones y los Beatles competían con lo que los adolescentes llamaban «música de papás y mamás», Ken Dodd, los Seekers, los Bachelors o Jim Reeves. La banda sonora de The Sound of Music encabezó la lista de LPs casi todo 1965 y 1966. Los adolescentes más jóvenes encontraban nuevos ídolos como los Walker Brothers, baladistas melodramáticos a lo Spector.

podcast.title: Birth and Early Life (1940)
podcast.body: Born Harry Webb in India in 1940 to a family of British descent who had lived there for generations, benefiting greatly from the British Empire. After Indian independence and partition following World War II, his family moved to Britain, a country they had never inhabited, where they found themselves homeless and jobless. They were forced to live in a single room of a three-bedroom house, with another family of eight occupying the other rooms. "Harry Webb, who was born in India in 1940, to a family who were of British descent, but who had been in India for a couple of generations."

podcast.title: "The British Elvis" (1964)
podcast.body: In 1964, Billboard magazine named Cliff Richard the number one recording artist in the world, surpassing Elvis Presley, leading him to be called "the British Elvis," which illustrates his immense popularity in Britain. "In 1964, Billboard magazine named Cliff Richard the number one recording artist in the world. Elvis Presley was number two."

podcast.title: Accent Development
podcast.body: He eventually shed his Anglo-Indian accent, developing a generic, regionless middle-class accent with a hint of mid-Atlantic, which later became a common media accent, replacing the previously dominant "received pronunciation." This neutral accent provided a distinct advantage when he became a pop star, as it didn't tie him to a specific region. "Webb's accent would later become almost the default for people in the media."

podcast.title: Band Lineup Changes Post-Debut
podcast.body: After his TV debut, Cliff ceased playing guitar while singing. Ian Sanwell transitioned to playing bass, and the group sought a new guitarist, resulting in Hank Marvin and Bruce Welch joining the band. "Cliff was no longer playing guitar while he sang, and the group also needed a bass player, so Ian Samuel switched a bass, and they went looking for a new guitarist."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Career Over Love
podcast.body: At the point of signing his recording contract, Cliff was in a relationship. However, he realized that to be perceived as available to teenage girls, a necessity for a rock and roll star, he had to end the relationship. His girlfriend understood his choice between his burgeoning career and their love. "he knew that if he was going to be a rock and roll star, he had to appear available to the teenage girls. So he dumped her."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Contrast on "Boy Meets Girls"
podcast.body: Cliff Richard was one of the performers featured on the British TV show "Boy Meets Girls." His presence on the show provided a stark contrast to Gene Vincent's "mean, moody leather-clad" appearance, making Vincent's image instantly captivating to audiences. "on a show like Boy Meets Girls, where the rest of the acts were people like Cliff Richard or Adam Faith, having a mean, moody leatherclad rock and roll on screen was instantly captivating."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Driven and Utilitarian Nature
podcast.body: He possessed an incredible drive and was willing to leverage anyone around him for precisely as long as they could assist him in achieving his goals. If musicians wished to play skiffle, he would play skiffle for the moment, demonstrating an adaptability to serve his ambition. "But on the other hand he was incredibly driven and was willing to make use of anyone around him for precisely as long as it would take for them to help him achieve his goals."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Elvis Presley Obsession
podcast.body: At 16, an Elvis Presley record profoundly changed his life, leading him to become obsessed with Elvis and strive to emulate his appearance. He later insisted on performing with an Elvis-style vocal imitation and hip thrusts, even when singing skiffle music. "Young Harry became obsessed with Elvis Presley, and tried to make himself look as much like Elvis as possible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Entry into Music via Terry Smart
podcast.body: After leaving school and failing nearly all his exams, he decided to pursue a career as a rock and roll star. His opportunity arose when his bike broke, forcing him to take a bus where he encountered his old school friend, Terry Smart, a drummer in a Skiffle group. Smart, whose group needed a new singer as theirs had been drafted, remembered Harry's singing ability and invited him to join. "On the same bus was an old school friend, Terry Smart, who was the drummer in a Skiffle group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Evolution to The Shadows
podcast.body: By Cliff Richard's 19th birthday, the only remaining original element of his backing band, The Drifters, was its name. This name too would soon change, as "Cliff Richard and the Drifters" became "Cliff Richard and The Shadows." "By Cliff's 19th birthday, the only thing left of the original drifters was the name, and soon that would change too, as Cliff Richard and the drifters became Cliff Richard and the shadows."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Experience with Racism
podcast.body: While he had benefited from racism in India, upon moving to Britain, he became a victim of it. Despite being white, his dark complexion, Anglo-Indian accent, and origin from India led schoolmates to mistakenly assume he was Indian and question him about his "week one," referencing caricatured depictions of Indians in cowboy films. "in Britain he was a victim of it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: First Public Performance
podcast.body: His initial public performance occurred with a vocal group he formed at school, where he performed a solo on the song "Harbbeke Hotel." "His first public performance was with a vocal group he formed at school, and he took a solo on Harbbeke Hotel."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Formation of The Drifters
podcast.body: While still performing with the Skiffle group, he secretly conspired with Terry Smart to form their own rock and roll group. His friend Norman Midham attended the Skiffle group's rehearsals, intently observing the guitarist to learn material for their new, clandestine group. After leaving the Dictig Skiffle group, Webb, Smart, and Midham officially formed "The Drifters." "Webb and Smart left the Dictig Skiffle group, and with Midham they formed a new rock-and-roll group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Ian Sanwell's Firing
podcast.body: Cliff secretly planned to replace Ian Sanwell with Jett Harris, a musician who had played with Hank Marvin and The Vipers. Sanwell's perceived musical shortcomings became apparent as Cliff began playing with more skilled musicians. Cliff did not inform Sanwell directly, instead delegating the task of firing him to John Foster. Sanwell later achieved success as a songwriter and record producer, notably producing "Horse with No Name" for the band America. "Cliff didn't tell Samuel himself. He got John Foster to fire him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: John Foster as Manager
podcast.body: John Foster, who worked at a sewage farm and lacked any prior music business experience, became the group's manager. His key qualifications in 1958 were possessing a telephone (a sign of importance) and having a casual acquaintance with the managers of The Two I's coffee bar, a famous music venue where he believed he could secure them a gig. "a man named John Foster came up and introduced himself to them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: John Foster's Departure
podcast.body: After Ian Sanwell's firing, John Foster, who had been the group's manager, was first demoted to roadie. Subsequently, he received two weeks' notice of termination in a letter written by Cliff's father, leading to his final departure from the group. "Shortly after that, Foster was gone as well, first demoted from manager to roadie, then given two weeks notice in a letter from Cliff's dad."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Media Outcry over Sexuality
podcast.body: Following his successful TV debut and the chart performance of "Move It," Cliff Richard faced a media storm regarding his " brazen sexuality." The enemy accused him of "crude exhibitionism," while the Daily Sketch ran a headline asking if he was "too sexy." "There was a media outcry over Cliff's brazen sexuality, with the enemy accusing him of crude exhibitionism, while the daily sketch would ask, is this boy TV star too sexy?"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Name Change to Cliff Richard
podcast.body: A booking agent, after seeing the group perform at The Two I's, wanted to book them as a lead singer backed by a group. He deemed "Harry Webb" an unsuitable name for a star, changing it to Cliff Richard, a name Harry Webb subsequently adopted fully in his personal life. "So the Drifters became Cliff Richard and the Drifters, and Harry Webb soon told everyone in his life that he was only to be addressed as Cliff from now on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Norman Midham's Departure
podcast.body: Ian Sanwell convinced Cliff that Norman Midham, who played rhythm guitar like Cliff, was redundant. Sanwell argued against having three guitarists and dividing the earnings three ways instead of two. Consequently, Midham, who had been friends with Cliff since childhood, was removed from the group. "So Mitham, who had been friends with Cliff since he were both nine, was out of the group."

podcast.title: Partnership with Olivia Newton-John
podcast.body: British star Cliff Richard partnered with Olivia Newton-John early in her career in England. She opened his concerts and was a frequent guest on his variety show, which helped maintain her visibility to the British public. "She opened his concerts and was a frequent guest on his variety show. It kept Livy visible to the British public."

podcast.title: Personal Habits
podcast.body: Even as a teenager, he maintained a strict code of conduct, refusing to smoke, drink, or use blasphemous language. He was known for his softly spoken manner. When asked if he had a girlfriend during his teenage years, he would produce a photograph of his mother from his pocket. "He refused to smoke, drink or blaspheme. He was very softly spoken, and as a teenager when asked if he had a girlfriend he would say, yes, I've got a picture of her in my pocket, I would pull out a photo of his mother."

podcast.title: Recording Contract Terms
podcast.body: For his first single recorded at Abbey Road Studios, only Cliff Richard's name was featured on the recording contract. While the record label would credit "Cliff Richard and the Drifters," the other group members were compensated only with a flat session fee, whereas Cliff alone received artist royalties. "But only Cliff Richard's name was on the recording contract."

podcast.title: Session Musicians for First Single
podcast.body: Given Cliff's limited guitar skills, Ian Sanwell switched to rhythm guitar for the first recording session, and session musician Ernie Sheer was brought in to play lead guitar. The group was further augmented in the studio by double bass player Frank Clark and the Mike Sam Singers for backing vocals. "Cliff didn't play guitar especially well, so for the session, Samuel switched to Rhythm, and the session player, Ernie Sheer, was brought into play lead."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Skiffle Group - Dictig Skiffle Group
podcast.body: He joined the Dictig Skiffle Group as their lead singer, diligently learning their material despite his personal musical tastes not aligning with skiffle. He controversially insisted on singing in an Elvis-style voice and thrusting his hips, a style that didn't suit the traditional skiffle songs. "So Harry Webb joined Dictig Skiffle Group and became their lead singer."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: TV Debut and Image
podcast.body: Made his television debut on "Oh Boy!" in September 1958, shortly before his 18th birthday. Jack Good insisted that Cliff perform "Move It" and personally coached him for a full week on every aspect of his performance, including specific blinks, gestures (like clutching his arm as if in pain), and how to look down instead of directly at the audience. Good also selected his shocking pink outfit (which was not visible on black and white TV but intended to excite the audience) and had his hair styled to be less like Elvis's. "Good work with Cliff for a full week on his performance of the song, instructing him in every blink, every time he should clutch his arm as if in pain, the way he should look down, not straight at the audience, everything."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Terry Smart's Replacement
podcast.body: Cliff replaced his childhood friend Terry Smart, who had initially invited him into the group, with Tony Meahin, another former member of The Vipers. "Cliff replaced Terry Smart, his old school friend, the person who had invited him into his group with Tony Meahin, another ex-viper."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: US Career vs. Olivia Newton-John's
podcast.body: Despite his massive popularity in Britain and shared manager (Peter Gormley) with Olivia Newton-John, Cliff Richard's career never fully took off in the US to the same extent as hers, despite hits like "We Don't Talk Anymore," "Dreaming," and "Devil Woman." "I honestly do not understand why Cliff Richard's career didn't take off more in the US."

podcast.title: Vehicle for Expresso Bongo Film
podcast.body: The film version of "Expresso Bongo," a rewritten satire of the British music industry, was made into a vehicle for Cliff Richard, with the satire removed and presented as a straight rags-to-riches story. "It was made into a vehicle for another singer who had been unregular at the two eyes."
